subject: ela
cluster: Range of reading and level of text complexity
intro: Each problem includes a dense informational passage at the upper end of the grades 6 to 8 complexity band. Read the whole passage carefully, then answer in complete sentences using evidence from the text. These questions ask you to weigh competing ideas, infer an author's purpose, or judge the best objective summary, so consider the passage as a whole before you decide.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

For most of human history, salt was as valuable as gold. Because the human body cannot survive without it, every society needed a steady supply, yet salt was hard to gather and harder to transport. In ancient times, people scraped it from dried lakebeds, boiled it out of seawater, or mined it from underground deposits left behind by oceans that vanished long ago. Whoever controlled these sources controlled a kind of wealth. Roman soldiers were sometimes paid partly in salt, and the English word salary comes from that practice. Trade routes thousands of miles long were built to carry salt across deserts, and entire cities grew up beside the mines and marshes that produced it. Kings taxed it heavily, knowing that no one could refuse to buy it. When refrigeration did not yet exist, salt was also the main way to keep meat and fish from spoiling, which meant it decided whether armies could march and whether ships could sail far from shore. Only in the last two hundred years, as mining and shipping grew cheap and easy, did salt finally become the ordinary, inexpensive thing it is today.

Which of the following best states the central idea that this passage as a whole develops, and what detail from the text most strongly supports your choice?
items.answer: The central idea is that for most of history salt was extremely valuable and powerful because people could not live without it yet it was difficult to obtain, and it became cheap only recently. The strongest supporting detail is that salt was 'as valuable as gold,' that kings taxed it heavily because no one could refuse to buy it, and that long trade routes and whole cities grew up to supply it.

steps: Look for the point the whole passage develops rather than any single fact. The opening compares salt to gold and the closing says it became ordinary only in the last two hundred years, framing the entire passage around salt's lost value.

Notice that nearly every sentence supports one idea: salt mattered enormously because the body needs it and it was hard to get (mining, boiling, long trade routes, heavy taxes, paying soldiers, preserving food).
Avoid summaries that restate just one detail, such as 'the word salary comes from salt' or 'salt preserved meat.' Those are supporting details, not the main point.

State the central idea: salt was once a source of great value and power because it was essential but scarce, and only recently became cheap. Cite the gold comparison and the heavy taxes as the strongest evidence because they show its value across the whole passage.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The ocean is far louder than most people imagine. Sound travels nearly five times faster in water than in air, and it carries for much greater distances, so the sea is filled with a constant background of noise. Some of this noise is natural: waves, cracking ice, rumbling underwater earthquakes, and the calls of whales and fish that use sound to find food and one another. In recent decades, though, human activity has added a new layer of noise. The engines of enormous cargo ships drone continuously, sonar pulses sweep across whole regions, and underwater blasts used to search for oil can be heard hundreds of miles away. Scientists who study marine life have grown worried. Many animals, especially whales and dolphins, depend on sound the way people depend on sight. When the water grows too noisy, these animals struggle to hear one another, lose track of their migration routes, and have trouble finding mates or food. Some researchers compare the problem to trying to hold a conversation in a room where the music keeps getting louder. The animals are not being struck or poisoned, yet their world is being filled with interference that did not exist a century ago.

What is the author's main purpose in writing this passage, and which part of the text reveals that purpose? Explain in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The author's main purpose is to inform readers and raise concern about how human-made noise in the ocean is harming marine animals that rely on sound. This purpose is revealed when the author explains that scientists 'have grown worried' and describes how whales and dolphins struggle to communicate, navigate, and find food when the water becomes too noisy.

steps: Determine purpose by asking why the author wrote the passage, not just what it says. The passage moves from explaining ocean sound to highlighting a growing human-caused problem.

Find the turning point: the phrase 'In recent decades, though, human activity has added a new layer of noise,' followed by 'Scientists ... have grown worried,' signals that the author wants readers to understand and care about a harmful change.
Reject a purpose that is too narrow, such as 'to explain that sound travels faster in water.' That fact is background, not the reason for the whole passage.
State the purpose as informing and concerning the reader about noise pollution harming marine life, and cite the 'scientists have grown worried' section as the clearest evidence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

In 1854, a deadly outbreak of cholera struck a neighborhood in London. At the time, most doctors believed the disease spread through bad-smelling air, a theory called miasma. A physician named John Snow doubted this idea. He suspected the illness was tied to something people were swallowing, not breathing. To test his hunch, Snow mapped every cholera death in the area, marking each one as a dot on a street plan. As the map filled in, a pattern appeared. The dots clustered tightly around a single public water pump on Broad Street, while neighborhoods that drew water elsewhere were largely spared. Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump's handle so no one could use it. New cases in the area soon fell. Snow could not yet see the bacteria that caused cholera, since microscopes powerful enough did not exist, but his careful mapping had revealed the path of the disease. For this work he is often called a founder of modern epidemiology, the science of tracking how illnesses spread through populations.

How is this passage mainly organized, and how does that structure help the reader understand John Snow's discovery? Answer in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The passage is organized mainly in chronological order, moving step by step from the 1854 outbreak, to Snow's doubt, to his mapping of deaths, to removing the pump handle, and finally to the drop in new cases. This sequence helps the reader follow how Snow reasoned and proved his idea, showing cause and effect in the order events actually happened so the discovery feels logical and earned.

steps: Trace the order of ideas. The passage gives a date, then a belief, then Snow's hypothesis, his experiment, the result, and the lasting outcome, all in time order.
Identify the structure as chronological (a sequence of events over time), with an element of cause and effect built into the sequence.
Avoid mislabeling it as compare and contrast just because miasma theory is mentioned. The miasma idea is only the starting point that Snow disproves; the passage is built on a timeline.
Explain that the chronological order lets the reader follow Snow's reasoning step by step, making clear how removing the pump handle led to fewer cases and why his method was important.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Many people assume that the tallest mountain on Earth is Mount Everest, but the answer depends on how you measure. Everest's peak reaches the highest point above sea level, about 8,849 meters, which is why it holds the famous record. Measured from base to summit, however, Everest is not the winner. The Hawaiian volcano Mauna Kea rises only about 4,200 meters above the sea, yet most of the mountain is hidden underwater. From its true base on the ocean floor to its top, Mauna Kea stands more than 10,000 meters tall, taller than Everest. There is yet another way to measure. Because the Earth bulges slightly at the equator, the peak of Mount Chimborazo in Ecuador, though far shorter above sea level than Everest, is actually the point on the planet's surface that sits farthest from the center of the Earth. Each of these mountains can fairly be called the tallest, depending on the starting point chosen. The disagreement is not about the mountains themselves, which have not changed, but about the meaning of a single word.

The passage says that 'the disagreement is not about the mountains themselves ... but about the meaning of a single word.' Based on the whole passage, which word is meant, and what point is the author making by ending this way? Explain in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The single word is 'tallest.' The author's point is that whether Everest, Mauna Kea, or Chimborazo counts as the tallest mountain depends entirely on how you define and measure tallest, so the answer changes with the starting point rather than with the mountains, which never change.

steps: Reread the passage's structure: it presents three mountains, each 'tallest' by a different measurement (above sea level, base to summit, distance from Earth's center).
Connect the closing sentence to that pattern. The 'single word' whose meaning causes the disagreement is 'tallest,' the word the whole passage has been redefining.
Identify the author's larger point: definitions and measurement methods shape the answer, so a question can have more than one correct answer depending on how a key term is understood.
State both parts: the word is 'tallest,' and the author is showing that the dispute comes from how that word is defined, not from any change in the mountains.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Honeybee colonies sometimes face a strange emergency: they suddenly have no queen. A queen may die, or a colony may grow so crowded that part of it must leave to start a new home. Without a queen to lay eggs, the colony will slowly die out, so the bees act quickly. Remarkably, worker bees can build a new queen from an ordinary egg. They choose a few young larvae that would otherwise have become ordinary workers and feed them an unusually rich food called royal jelly. Every larva eats some royal jelly at first, but the chosen ones receive it in great quantity and for much longer. This flood of royal jelly switches on a different set of instructions inside the larva's body. Instead of developing into a small worker, the larva grows larger, develops working ovaries, and emerges as a fertile queen capable of laying thousands of eggs. The genes inside the worker larva and the future queen are identical. The difference between a humble worker and the mother of the entire colony comes down almost entirely to diet during those first few days of life.

Using context, determine the meaning of the phrase 'switches on a different set of instructions' as it is used in this passage, and explain what evidence in the text supports your interpretation. Answer in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The phrase means that the rich royal jelly activates a different pattern of development inside the larva's body, causing it to grow into a queen instead of a worker. The text supports this because it explains that the same identical genes can produce either a worker or a fertile queen, and that the flood of royal jelly is what makes the larva develop a larger body and working ovaries.

steps: Locate the phrase and read the sentences around it. The royal jelly 'switches on a different set of instructions,' and then the larva develops into a queen rather than a worker.
Use the clue that 'the genes inside the worker larva and the future queen are identical,' so the instructions are biological directions for development, not new genes.
Interpret the phrase: the diet activates an alternate developmental pathway already present in the larva, turning it into a queen.
Support the reading with the detail that the larva 'grows larger, develops working ovaries, and emerges as a fertile queen,' which is the different outcome those activated instructions produce.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

When a volcano in Indonesia named Tambora erupted in April 1815, it threw so much ash and gas into the sky that the effects reached around the world. The eruption was one of the most powerful in recorded history. Tiny particles from the blast rose high into the atmosphere and spread across the globe, where they reflected part of the sun's light back into space. With less sunlight reaching the ground, temperatures dropped. The following year, 1816, became known across Europe and North America as the Year Without a Summer. Snow fell in June in some regions. Frost killed crops in July and August, and harvests failed. Food grew scarce and expensive, and in many places people went hungry. Some historians have even linked the gloomy, cold weather of that summer to the writing of a famous horror novel, composed indoors by writers trapped by the endless rain. Few people at the time understood that a single eruption on the far side of the planet had darkened their skies and ruined their crops. The connection between the volcano and the strange weather was not clearly recognized until long afterward.

What can the reader most reasonably conclude about why the people living through 1816 did not blame the volcano for their suffering? Support your conclusion with evidence from the passage. Answer in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The reader can reasonably conclude that the people did not blame the volcano because they had no way to know that an eruption so far away could affect their weather and crops. The passage supports this by stating that 'few people at the time understood that a single eruption on the far side of the planet had darkened their skies,' and that the connection was not clearly recognized until long afterward.

steps: Identify what the question asks: an inference about why people did not connect the volcano to their hardship.

Find the relevant evidence: 'Few people at the time understood that a single eruption on the far side of the planet had darkened their skies and ruined their crops,' and the connection 'was not clearly recognized until long afterward.'
Reason from the evidence: the eruption happened on the other side of the world, so the people lacked the knowledge to link distant events, an inference the text invites but does not state outright.
State the conclusion with support: people could not see the connection because the cause was too far away and not yet understood, as the closing sentences make clear.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Electric cars are often praised as a clean replacement for gasoline vehicles, and in important ways they are. They produce no exhaust from a tailpipe, so they do not pollute the air of the streets they drive on. Yet calling them perfectly clean overlooks a more complicated picture. The electricity that charges them has to come from somewhere, and in many regions that power is still generated by burning coal or natural gas. An electric car charged from a coal-heavy grid can be responsible for nearly as much pollution as an efficient gasoline car, just released at a power plant instead of on the road. The batteries raise concerns too. Building them requires mining metals such as lithium and cobalt, work that can damage land and water and that sometimes relies on harsh labor conditions. None of this means electric cars are a bad idea. As more electricity comes from wind and solar power, and as battery recycling improves, their advantages grow. But the honest answer is that an electric car is only as clean as the system that powers and builds it. Treating the cars as automatically pollution-free hides the real choices that still have to be made.

Which statement from this passage expresses the author's opinion or claim rather than a checkable fact, and how can you tell? Explain in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The statement 'an electric car is only as clean as the system that powers and builds it' expresses the author's claim, as does the judgment that calling electric cars 'perfectly clean overlooks a more complicated picture.' You can tell because these are conclusions the author is arguing for and asking the reader to accept, unlike checkable facts such as electric cars producing no tailpipe exhaust or batteries requiring mining of lithium and cobalt.

steps: Separate verifiable facts from the author's judgments. Facts in the passage include 'they produce no exhaust from a tailpipe' and 'building them requires mining metals such as lithium and cobalt.'
Find the sentences that state a position the author wants readers to accept, such as the cars being 'only as clean as the system that powers and builds it.' This is a claim, not a measurable fact.
Explain the test: a fact can be checked or measured, while a claim or opinion is an interpretation or judgment the author argues for.

Name the claim and justify it: the 'only as clean as the system' statement and the idea that treating the cars as clean 'overlooks a more complicated picture' are the author's arguments, supported by the facts but not facts themselves.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The deep sea is one of the least explored places on Earth, harder to reach in some ways than the surface of the Moon. Below about a thousand meters, sunlight vanishes completely and the water grows bitterly cold. The pressure becomes crushing, hundreds of times greater than at the surface, enough to collapse an ordinary submarine. For a long time, scientists assumed almost nothing could live there. They were wrong. Strange creatures thrive in the dark, many of them making their own light through a chemical reaction in their bodies, a trick called bioluminescence. Some fish dangle glowing lures to attract prey. Others flash light to confuse predators or to signal a mate. In 1977, researchers exploring the deep ocean floor made an even more startling discovery. Around cracks in the seabed, hot mineral-rich water poured out, and entire communities of life clustered there. These creatures did not depend on sunlight at all. Instead, bacteria at the base of the food chain turned chemicals from the vents into energy, a process called chemosynthesis. The finding overturned a basic assumption, since scientists had long believed that all life on Earth ultimately depended on the energy of the sun.

Explain how the discovery described in the second half of the passage changes the idea presented in the first half. In other words, how does the passage build from beginning to end? Answer in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The passage builds from the early assumption that almost nothing could survive in the crushing, sunless deep sea to the discovery that life not only survives there but can exist completely without sunlight. The 1977 vent discovery, where bacteria use chemosynthesis to turn chemicals into energy, overturns the long-held belief that all life on Earth depends on the sun, so the second half corrects and deepens the idea set up in the first half.

steps: Track how the ideas develop. The first half sets up a belief: the deep sea is so harsh that 'almost nothing could live there,' and all life depends on the sun.
Identify the shift: 'They were wrong.' The passage then describes bioluminescent creatures and, more importantly, the 1977 vent communities that live without sunlight.
Connect the two halves: the discovery of chemosynthesis 'overturned a basic assumption' that all life depends on the sun's energy.
Explain the build: the passage moves from a confident assumption to evidence that disproves it, so each part of the second half corrects and expands the idea introduced at the start.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

In the 1930s, large parts of the American Great Plains turned to dust. Years of drought dried out the soil, but drought alone did not cause the disaster. For decades, farmers had plowed up the deep-rooted prairie grasses that once held the ground in place, replacing them with crops like wheat. The grasses had survived dry spells for thousands of years because their roots locked the soil down. When the rains failed and the crops withered, there was nothing left to anchor the bare earth. Powerful winds lifted the loose soil into the air, forming enormous dark clouds of dust that buried fences, darkened the sky at noon, and choked people and animals. Some storms carried Plains soil as far as the East Coast. Thousands of families, unable to farm or even breathe safely, packed what they could and left, becoming refugees within their own country. The period came to be called the Dust Bowl. It taught a hard lesson about how human choices and natural forces can combine to create a catastrophe that neither would have produced alone.

According to this passage, the Dust Bowl had more than one cause. Explain how a natural cause and a human cause combined to produce the disaster, using evidence from the text. Answer in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The natural cause was a long drought that dried out the soil and killed the crops, and the human cause was that farmers had plowed up the deep-rooted prairie grasses whose roots once held the soil in place. The two combined because, once the drought left the ground bare and there were no grass roots to anchor it, powerful winds lifted the loose soil into huge dust storms, a catastrophe the passage says 'neither would have produced alone.'

steps: Find both causes the passage names. The natural cause is the drought: 'Years of drought dried out the soil.' The human cause is plowing up the prairie grasses that held the soil.
Show how they combine: the grasses' roots used to anchor the soil through dry spells, but with them gone and the crops dead, 'there was nothing left to anchor the bare earth.'
Cite the result: winds lifted the loose soil into dust storms, and note the passage's own statement that this was a disaster 'that neither would have produced alone.'
Avoid blaming only the drought or only the farming. The passage stresses that the cause was the combination of the two.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Languages, like living things, can die. A language is considered extinct when its last fluent speaker passes away and no one is left who learned it as a first tongue. This is happening faster today than ever before. Experts estimate that of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken on Earth, nearly half may disappear within this century. The reasons are tangled together. As people move to cities for work, they often adopt a dominant national language, and their children grow up speaking it instead of the language of their grandparents. Schools, television, and the internet usually operate in a handful of major languages, which makes smaller ones seem less useful. When a language vanishes, more is lost than a set of words. Each language carries unique knowledge, including names for local plants and medicines, stories passed down for generations, and ways of describing the world that exist nowhere else. For this reason, some communities are working hard to record their elders, teach children, and bring endangered languages back into daily life. Whether these efforts can outpace the loss remains uncertain, but the people leading them argue that saving a language means saving a way of seeing.

Write an objective summary of this passage in two or three sentences. Your summary should state the main idea and key points without adding your own opinion.
items.answer: Languages can become extinct when their last fluent speakers die, and nearly half of the world's roughly seven thousand languages may disappear this century as people shift to dominant national languages used in cities, schools, and media. The passage explains that losing a language also means losing unique knowledge, stories, and ways of seeing the world. Because of this, some communities are working to record elders and teach children in order to keep endangered languages alive, though it is uncertain whether they will succeed.

steps: Identify the central idea: many languages are dying quickly, and their loss takes valuable knowledge with them, prompting efforts to save them.

Select the key supporting points: the definition of extinction, the scale (half of seven thousand may vanish), the causes (moving to cities, dominant languages in schools and media), what is lost, and the revival efforts.
Leave out personal opinion. Do not write 'this is the saddest thing' or 'people should care more.' Restate only what the passage says.
Combine the main idea and key points into a brief, neutral summary in your own words rather than copying sentences.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The idea of a public park open to everyone was once unusual. In the middle of the 1800s, the city of New York was growing rapidly, packed with buildings and people, with little open green space for ordinary residents. Wealthy families could escape to the countryside, but most people could not. A few reformers argued that a great park, free and open to all, would improve the health and spirits of the whole city. The plan was controversial. Critics complained that it would cost too much and that the chosen land, rocky and swampy, was nearly worthless. Yet the city pressed ahead. Designers reshaped the ground entirely, hauling in soil, planting hundreds of thousands of trees and shrubs, and carving out lakes and winding paths. What looks today like untouched nature in Central Park is almost entirely artificial, built by human hands. The park became a model copied by cities around the world. Its planners believed that access to nature should not be a privilege reserved for the rich, and that a shared green space could bring a divided, crowded city together.

What does the passage suggest was the planners' main reason for building Central Park, and how does the detail that the park 'is almost entirely artificial' deepen the reader's understanding of that goal? Answer in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The passage suggests the planners' main reason was to give all city residents, not just the wealthy, free access to nature that would improve their health and bring a crowded, divided city together. The detail that the park is almost entirely artificial deepens this understanding by showing how committed the planners were to that goal, since they reshaped worthless, rocky, swampy land and hauled in soil and trees to create natural-looking space for everyone.

steps: Identify the planners' goal from the text: 'access to nature should not be a privilege reserved for the rich,' and a shared green space could 'bring a divided, crowded city together.'
Consider the 'almost entirely artificial' detail in light of that goal. The land was 'rocky and swampy' and called 'nearly worthless,' yet they rebuilt it completely.
Connect the two: the immense effort to manufacture a natural-looking park shows how seriously the planners pursued the goal of giving ordinary people access to nature.
State both parts: the main reason (free nature for all, uniting the city) and how the artificial-construction detail underscores the planners' commitment.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

A student reading the passage below was asked to summarize it and wrote: 'Wolves are scary predators that kill lots of animals, so it is good that they almost disappeared.' Read the passage and explain why that summary is not accurate or objective.

Passage: When wolves were removed from Yellowstone National Park in the early 1900s, few people expected the chain of effects that followed. With no wolves to hunt them, the park's elk multiplied and grazed freely. They ate young willow and aspen trees along the rivers faster than the trees could grow back. As those trees vanished, songbirds lost nesting places and beavers lost the wood they needed to build dams. The riverbanks, no longer held together by roots, began to erode. Decades later, in 1995, wolves were brought back. Slowly, the changes began to reverse. The elk grew more cautious and stopped lingering in the open river valleys. Young trees returned, the birds and beavers came back, and the rivers grew healthier. Scientists use the word that describes a species whose presence shapes an entire ecosystem: a keystone species. The wolves' return showed that removing a single predator can unravel a whole web of life, and that restoring it can help weave that web back together.

Explain in three or four sentences why the student's summary is inaccurate and not objective, using evidence from the passage.
items.answer: The student's summary is inaccurate because the passage shows the opposite of what the student claims: removing wolves harmed Yellowstone, since elk overgrazed the young trees, songbirds and beavers lost their habitats, and the riverbanks eroded. It is also not objective because the student inserts personal opinion ('scary predators' and 'it is good that they almost disappeared') instead of neutrally restating the text. An accurate, objective summary would explain that wolves are a keystone species whose removal unraveled the ecosystem and whose return in 1995 helped restore the trees, animals, and rivers.

steps: Compare the student's claim to the passage. The student says it was 'good' that wolves nearly disappeared, but the passage shows their removal caused overgrazing, lost habitat, and eroding rivers.
Spot the inserted opinion: words like 'scary' and the judgment 'it is good' are the reader's feelings, not the passage's neutral information. An objective summary avoids them.
Identify the passage's actual main idea: wolves are a keystone species, and removing them unraveled the ecosystem while restoring them helped repair it.
Explain both flaws clearly: the summary states the wrong conclusion and adds personal judgment, so it is neither accurate nor objective.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

For centuries, sailors crossing the open ocean faced a deadly puzzle. They could find their latitude, their position north or south, by measuring the height of the sun or stars. But finding longitude, their position east or west, defeated the finest minds in Europe. Ships ran aground or wandered for weeks off course because no one could reliably tell how far east or west they had traveled. The key, scientists realized, was time. If a sailor knew the exact time at a fixed home port and compared it to the local time at sea, the difference would reveal the longitude. The trouble was that no clock could keep accurate time on a rolling, damp, temperature-changing ship. Pendulum clocks, which worked on land, were useless at sea. In the 1700s, a self-taught English carpenter named John Harrison devoted his life to the problem. After decades of work, he built a compact, rugged timepiece that kept near-perfect time despite the ship's motion and the changing weather. With Harrison's clock, sailors could finally fix their longitude, and ocean voyages became far safer. A problem that had stumped famous astronomers was solved by a craftsman building a better machine.

This passage is built around a problem and its solution. State the problem and the solution clearly, and explain why the writer notes that the solution came from 'a self-taught English carpenter' rather than from 'famous astronomers.' Answer in three or four sentences.
items.answer: The problem was that sailors could not reliably determine their longitude, their east-to-west position, which caused ships to run aground or wander off course. The solution was John Harrison's compact, rugged clock, which kept accurate time at sea so sailors could compare home-port time to local time and calculate their longitude. The writer stresses that Harrison was a self-taught carpenter, not a famous astronomer, to highlight that the breakthrough came from practical craftsmanship and building a better machine rather than from the theoretical experts who had failed, making the achievement surprising and noteworthy.

steps: Identify the problem the passage sets up: sailors could not find their longitude, so ships got lost or wrecked.
Identify the solution: Harrison's sea-worthy clock let sailors compare times and finally fix their longitude.
Notice the contrast the writer draws between 'famous astronomers' who failed and a 'self-taught carpenter' who succeeded.
Explain the point of that contrast: it emphasizes that practical skill solved a problem the experts could not, which is part of why the writer finds the story remarkable.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Every year, monarch butterflies make one of the most astonishing journeys in nature. Each fall, millions of them leave the northern United States and Canada and travel thousands of miles south to a small region of forest in central Mexico, where they gather in such numbers that they bend the branches of the trees. What makes the journey so puzzling is that no single butterfly knows the way. A monarch lives only a few weeks, so the insects that arrive in Mexico are the great-great-grandchildren of the ones that left it the previous spring. The route is not taught or remembered. Instead, the knowledge is somehow carried in the monarchs' genes, guiding each new generation along a path it has never seen. Scientists are still working out exactly how the butterflies navigate. They appear to use the position of the sun, adjusting for the time of day with a kind of internal clock, and they may also sense the Earth's magnetic field. Loss of habitat now threatens the migration, as the forests where they spend the winter shrink and the milkweed plants their young depend on grow scarcer. Protecting both ends of their long journey, scientists warn, is the only way to keep this generations-long relay from breaking.

The passage calls the migration a 'generations-long relay.' Based on the whole passage, explain what this comparison means and why it fits the monarchs' journey. Answer in two or three sentences.
items.answer: The comparison means that no single butterfly completes the whole migration; instead, the journey is passed along through several short-lived generations the way runners pass a baton in a relay race. It fits because a monarch lives only a few weeks, so the butterflies that reach Mexico are the great-great-grandchildren of the ones that left, and each new generation continues a path it has never seen, carried in its genes rather than learned.

steps: Understand the comparison: in a relay, different runners each cover one leg and hand off to the next. The passage applies this to the migration.
Find the supporting detail: 'A monarch lives only a few weeks,' so 'the insects that arrive in Mexico are the great-great-grandchildren of the ones that left.'
Connect the figure of speech to the facts: no one butterfly makes the full trip; generations take turns continuing it, with the route carried in their genes.
Explain why 'relay' fits: it captures how the journey is completed by a series of generations passing the migration along rather than by any single traveler.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

At first glance, a coral reef looks like a colorful underwater rock garden, but it is alive in a surprising way. The hard structure of a reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps, each no larger than a pencil eraser. These polyps live in vast colonies and slowly produce a stony skeleton that, over thousands of years, grows into a reef. Inside the soft body of each polyp lives an even tinier partner: a type of algae. The two depend on each other completely. The algae use sunlight to make food and share much of it with the coral, while the coral gives the algae a protected place to live and the raw materials they need. This partnership also gives the reef its brilliant colors. When the ocean grows too warm, however, the relationship breaks down. The stressed coral expels the algae living inside it, turning ghostly white, an event called bleaching. Without its algae partner, the coral loses its main food source. If the warm conditions last too long, the coral starves and dies, and the reef that took millennia to build can collapse in only a few years. Reefs shelter a quarter of all ocean species, so their loss would ripple far beyond the coral itself.

Based on the whole passage, explain the cause-and-effect chain that leads from warm ocean water to the possible collapse of a coral reef. Include at least three linked steps and use evidence from the text. Answer in three or four sentences.
items.answer: When the ocean grows too warm, the stressed coral expels the algae living inside it, which causes bleaching and turns the coral ghostly white. Because the algae had been making food and sharing it with the coral, losing them means the coral loses its main food source. If the warm conditions last too long, the coral starves and dies, and since reefs take thousands of years to build, the whole reef can collapse in only a few years, which the passage warns would ripple out because reefs shelter a quarter of all ocean species.
